title: Glasses of sugarcane juice: which group's share is larger?
description: Glasses of sugarcane juice are divided equally among children in two pairs of groups. The board writes equivalent fractions until the fractional units match, and then compares the number of units. Keeko doubts the answer by saying the group with more glasses always gets more.
teaching_notes: One idea: shares can be compared only when they use the same fractional unit, and when the number of children is the same this is already true. Watch for students who decide by the number of glasses alone.

source: Decide in which of the two groups each child gets a larger s
video_script.why: A learner compares two shares by writing equivalent fractions with the same fractional unit, and sees why equal numbers of children make the comparison easier.
video_script.substitution: the book's own groups: three glasses among four children against seven glasses among ten children, and four against five glasses among seven children
video_script.anchor: glasses of sugarcane juice divided equally among children
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the ten children get more because seven glasses is more than three glasses, and ignores that ten children share them.
video_script.payoff_line: each child in the first group gets more

final_answer.value: First pair: first group, 3/4 > 7/10; second pair: second group, 5/7 > 4/7; the second pair is easier because the number of children is the same
final_answer.spoken: in the first pair the first group gets more, and in the second pair the second group gets more, and the second pair was easier to compare

video_script.fraction_reading: three fourths, seven tenths, fifteen twentieths, fourteen twentieths, four sevenths, five sevenths

names.Jia: the child who insists on the same fractional unit
names.Leeza: the child who writes the equivalent fractions

never_show: a tick on the group with more glasses before the working
maths_rules: pair 1, group 1: 3 glasses among 4 children, each child gets 3/4 glass
pair 1, group 2: 7 glasses among 10 children, each child gets 7/10 glass
15/20 > 14/20, so 3/4 > 7/10 and each child in group 1 gets more
pair 2: 4/7 and 5/7 have the same bottom number 7, and 5 > 4, so 5/7 > 4/7 and group 2 gets more
pair 2 is easier because the number of children is the same, so no equivalent fractions are needed
slip: Keeko says the ten children get more because 7 glasses is more than 3 glasses; but 10 children share them
video_script.design: Two pairs of groups of sugarcane juice. The first pair needs equivalent fractions until the bottom numbers match, at twenty. The second pair needs none because seven children are in both groups.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; group 1: four children with three glasses of sugarcane juice; group 2: ten children with seven glasses; the words in which group does each child get more? appear

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.g1: four children and three glasses of sugarcane juice appear on the left
marks.g2: ten children and seven glasses appear on the right
marks.ask: the words in which group does each child get more? appear

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, and it is about sugarcane juice.
<bookmark mark='g1'/>In one group, three glasses are divided equally among four children.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>In the other group, seven glasses are divided equally among ten children.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>In which group will each child get a larger share?

beats.on_screen: the two groups hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the shares 3/4 and 7/10 sit side by side; the bottom numbers 4 and 10 are circled in different colours; a fraction strip cut in fourths sits beside a strip cut in tenths

marks.unit: the shares 3/4 and 7/10 sit side by side with the bottom numbers circled
marks.strips: a strip cut in fourths sits beside a strip cut in tenths, and the pieces differ in size

narration: <bookmark mark='unit'/>Three fourths and seven tenths use different fractional units, because the bottom numbers differ.
<bookmark mark='strips'/>Fourths and tenths are pieces of different sizes. We cannot compare them by counting pieces.

beats.on_screen: Given: pair 1: 3 glasses among 4 children, 7 glasses among 10 children; pair 2: 4 glasses among 7 children, 5 glasses among 7 children
narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Given, three glasses are shared among four children, and seven glasses among ten children.
<bookmark mark='second'/>In the second pair, four glasses go to seven children, and five glasses to seven children.

beats.on_screen: To find: in each pair, the group where each child gets more; and which pair was easier to compare
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the group where each child gets more, in both pairs. We also say which pair was easier to compare.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: pair 1 shares: 3/4 and 7/10; the fractional unit must be the same

marks.shares: the shares 3/4 and 7/10 are written with a question mark between them
marks.unit: the words same fractional unit are written

narration: <bookmark mark='shares'/>Step one, write each share as a fraction. In the first pair, the shares are three fourths and seven tenths.
<bookmark mark='unit'/>Jia reminds us that both must use the same fractional unit.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12 = 12/16 = 15/20; 7/10 = 14/20; both have the bottom number 20

marks.list: the equivalent fractions of 3/4 are written one after another
marks.meet: 7/10 changes to 14/20 and the two bottom numbers 20 are circled

beats.colours: the common bottom number 20 = accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Step two, Leeza writes equivalent fractions of three fourths. They are six eighths, nine twelfths, twelve sixteenths, and fifteen twentieths.
<bookmark mark='meet'/>Seven tenths is also fourteen twentieths. Both bottom numbers are now twenty.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: both shares in twentieths; compare the numbers of twentieths: 15 and 14

marks.cmp: 15 twentieth pieces and 14 twentieth pieces are lined up one above the other

narration: <bookmark mark='cmp'/>Step three, both shares are counted in twentieths. We compare fifteen and fourteen, and fifteen is more.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: pair 2: 4/7 and 5/7; the bottom number 7 is the same, so compare 4 and 5; 5 > 4; no equivalent fractions needed

marks.same: 4/7 and 5/7 are written with the same bottom number circled
marks.easy: the words same number of children, easier are written

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Step four, the second pair is four sevenths and five sevenths. Both groups have seven children, so the unit is already the same.
<bookmark mark='easy'/>We only compare four and five, and five is more.

beats.on_screen: Answer: pair 1: 15/20 > 14/20, so 3/4 > 7/10, group 1; pair 2: 5/7 > 4/7, group 2; pair 2 is easier because the number of children is the same

marks.first: 3/4 > 7/10 is written and group 1 of pair 1 is boxed
marks.second: 5/7 > 4/7 is written and group 2 of pair 2 is boxed
marks.easy: the words pair 2 is easier are written

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>In the first pair, each child in the first group gets more.
<bookmark mark='second'/>In the second pair, each child in the second group gets more.
<bookmark mark='easy'/>The second pair was easier, because the number of children is the same.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the two groups
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble says the 10 children get more because 7 glasses is more than 3; the 10 children light up beside their 7 glasses; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: the bubble with the wrong idea appears
marks.more: the ten children light up beside their seven glasses
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and 15/20 and 14/20 appear again

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the ten children get more, because seven glasses is more than three glasses.
<bookmark mark='more'/>There are more glasses, but there are also many more children sharing them.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Counting glasses alone cannot tell us each share. We make the units the same first.
